overview: Port Eynon is a small village at the end of the road on the south Gower, where a sandy bay curves east to the neighbouring village of Horton about half a mile away. Behind the beach are a pay car park, toilets, cafés, a campsite and a pub, and a slipway is used to launch dive and sailing boats. The village is small, so in summer the car park is the easiest way in.

It is a classic family beach, with a wide stretch of sand and rock pools to explore at low tide, and RNLI lifeguards in the summer holidays. The village sits inside the Gower's Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty and on the Wales Coast Path. Dogs are allowed all year on the western part of the beach, from the main steps to the Salt House, but are banned east of the steps from May to September. Swim between the red and yellow flags when the lifeguards are on.

There is plenty of history. A lifeboat ran from here until 1919; three young crewmen died in 1916 going to the SS Dunvegan, and their memorial is in the churchyard. Along the point are the ruined Salt House and the old dovecote of Culver Hole. Culver Hole is a Grade II listed scheduled monument, and the youth hostel at the south end of the bay is a converted lifeboat house.

text: Port Eynon faces south and needs a solid south-westerly swell to break. When it works the waves are gentle and good for learners and longboarders, and when Llangennith is too big it can be the sensible choice.
Lower tides open up more sand and the rock pools at the edges; keep clear of the rocks and, in season, stay between the red and yellow flags.

Port Eynon only works when conditions are just right, and summer is nearly always flat. It's a fairly exposed beach break with lefts and rights, best on a south-westerly groundswell with a north-westerly offshore, and best around low tide. It's unlikely to be crowded even when it's up. February gives the best odds, but clean days are rare.

cards.text: Rocks at both ends, and lifeguards only on set dates — no flags means no lifeguards.

practical.label: Parking
practical.title: Pay car park
practical.text: Behind the beach, with disabled spaces.

practical.label: Facilities
practical.title: Toilets and first aid
practical.text: Accessible toilets, a lifeguard station and first aid post, cafés, a pub and village shops.

practical.label: Lifeguards
practical.title: Summer holidays
practical.text: In 2026 the RNLI patrolled 23–31 May, weekends 6–28 June, and daily 4 July–6 September, 10am–6pm.

practical.label: Dogs
practical.title: Part-beach summer ban
practical.text: Dogs are allowed all year from the main steps west to the Salt House. From the steps east to the Horton beach access they are banned 1 May–30 September.

practical.label: History
practical.title: Salt House and Culver Hole
practical.text: Both lie west of the village around Port Eynon Point, reached on the coast path.

faqs.q: Are there lifeguards at Port Eynon?
faqs.a: Yes, in season. In 2026 that was 23–31 May, weekends in June, and daily from 4 July to 6 September, 10am–6pm.

faqs.q: Can I take my dog to Port Eynon?
faqs.a: Yes, west of the main steps towards the Salt House all year. East of the steps to Horton, dogs are banned from 1 May to 30 September.
Yes, Horton is about half a mile along the beach to the east.

faqs.q: Is Port Eynon good for surfing?
faqs.a: Only with a solid south-west swell, when it suits learners and longboarders.
